newsitem.title: UK: Enron chief sees boom in Europe gas market.
newsitem.headline: Enron chief sees boom in Europe gas market.

text.p: Europe's natural gas market is set for phenomenal growth and will be worth $250 billion by the end of the next decade, bigger than the fast-growing market in the United States, Enron Corp. Chairman Kenneth Lay said Monday.

"Within the next five years there will be a $100 billion retail market in Europe and by the middle or end of next decade the retail and wholesale markets will be worth $250 billion," Lay said in an interview.
He said the combined retail electricity and natural gas market, worth $3 billion in the United States currently, would grow to $150 billion by 2001.
Lay said he was encouraged by the progress made opening up the energy market in parts of Europe other than Britain. He saw the European Commission talking of phasing in deregulation over nine years.
Markets in the United States are gradually being deregulated.
"We're in favour of a more accelerated schedule," he said. "It's hard to imagine how any one country can hold out."
"Germany will probably be first," Lay continued, but added that progress has also been made in the Netherlands.
"It's irresistible in that it results in much lower energy costs," he said. "I've yet to see any market where competition led to higher prices."
The Houston-based gas and energy company is already active across Europe.
It supplies up to 4 percent of Britain's electricity through its Teesside power station in Northeast England, and in March will start work on a plant in Lincolnshire in the East.
Enron also has stakes in plants in former East Germany and Sardinia, and a planned plant in Turkey.
But the company has also been dogged by a legal dispute over North Sea gas supply.

One of Enron's biggest competitors is American Electric Power Co. Inc., which said Monday it agreed to acquire Britain's Yorkshire Electricity Group Plc for about $2.4 billion in a bid with another U.S. utility.
Lay would not comment on the acquisition, other than to say "the main question is one of timing. If there's a change of government, the matter will be taken up by the new government."
